reconciled_candidates.label: Problem Framing Definition and Importance
reconciled_candidates.description: Problem framing is the process of discovering and defining the real problem before seeking solutions. It is distinct from problem solving, and identifying the right problem is more critical than solving it well.
coverage_criteria: Student can define problem framing.
Student can differentiate problem framing from problem solving.
Student can articulate why problem identification takes precedence over problem solving.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates all emphasize that defining the right problem is the foundational step. The definition, the contrast with problem solving, and the primacy of problem identification are inseparable components of the same core message.

reconciled_candidates.label: Cognitive Biases that Lead to Premature Convergence
reconciled_candidates.description: Premature convergence is the tendency to jump to solutions quickly, driven by pattern completion and confirmation bias. These cognitive mechanisms cause people to settle on the first plausible answer without fully understanding the problem.
coverage_criteria: Student can define premature convergence.
Student can explain how pattern completion and confirmation bias contribute to premature convergence.
Student can identify an example of each bias in a problem-framing scenario.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These three candidates describe the same phenomenon from the neuroscience perspective, with pattern completion and confirmation bias as specific manifestations of premature convergence. Together they form a coherent lesson on why people skip framing.

reconciled_candidates.label: Organizational Pressures that Reinforce Solution-Jumping

reconciled_candidates.label: Double Diamond Model for Problem Framing
reconciled_candidates.description: The Double Diamond model is a framework for problem framing consisting of two phases: Discover (divergent thinking to explore the problem space) and Define (convergent thinking to crystallize the problem).
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the Discover and Define phases.
Student can explain why divergent and convergent thinking are both necessary for effective problem framing.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate introduces a structured model; it is a standalone concept that can be taught independently.

reconciled_candidates.label: Problem Reframing Technique
reconciled_candidates.description: Problem reframing is the deliberate restating of a strategic question to expose new perspectives, risks, and opportunities. reconciled_candidates.label: Impact of Poor Framing on AI Effectiveness

reconciled_candidates.label: Description Invariance
reconciled_candidates.description: A normative principle of classical decision theory stating that rational agents' choices should not depend on the particular way options are described, as long as the descriptions are logically equivalent.
coverage_criteria: Define description invariance and explain why it is important for rational decision-making.
Identify a scenario where description invariance is violated.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate uniquely introduces description invariance, a foundational concept.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The abstract explicitly defines description invariance as a tenet of classic decision theory and contrasts it with the demonstrated failure due to framing.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational definition that can be checked with 1-2 recall and comprehension questions.

reconciled_candidates.label: Framing Effects and Preference Reversals
reconciled_candidates.description: Framing effects occur when different but logically equivalent descriptions of a decision problem lead to systematic preference reversals, violating description invariance. For example, people tend to be risk-averse when options are framed as gains and risk-seeking when framed as losses.
coverage_criteria: Define framing effect and give an example (e.g., Asian disease problem).
Explain how framing leads to preference reversals in decisions under risk.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These two candidates describe the framing effect phenomenon and its direct outcome of preference reversals, which together form a single teachable concept about how framing changes choices.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The abstract states that framing research has demonstrated a failure of description invariance and that different descriptions frequently lead to preference reversals.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This central concept can be assessed with 2-3 questions, including definitions and examples.

lesson.title: Problem framing
lesson.description: This class combines theoretical references on decision-making frameworks and the balance between data and intuition with a practical group exercise. Students analyze the strategic dilemma of a rapidly growing Brazilian startup and must decide between international expansion, investment in new technology, or local consolidation. The dynamic challenges the groups to justify their choice, identify critical information, and reflect on when to rely on objective evidence or managerial instincts.
